title: Chapter 68 — The Blanket
paragraphs: I have paid no small attention to that much-disputed subject, the skin of the whale. I have argued about it with seasoned whalemen at sea and with learned naturalists on land. My original opinion has not changed — but it is only an opinion.

The question is this: what is the whale's skin, and where is it? You already know what his blubber is. It has roughly the texture of firm, close-grained beef, only tougher, more elastic and more compact, and it runs from eight or ten to twelve and fifteen inches thick.

Now, however absurd it may seem at first to speak of any creature's skin as being of that sort of consistency and thickness, in point of fact these are no arguments against such a presumption; because you cannot raise any other dense enveloping layer from the whale's body except that same blubber; and the outermost enveloping layer of any animal, if reasonably dense, what can that be but the skin? True, from the unmarred dead body of the whale you may scrape off with your hand an infinitely thin, transparent substance, somewhat like the thinnest shreds of isinglass (a clear gelatin made from fish bladders), only it is almost as flexible and soft as satin — that is, before it is dried, when it not only contracts and thickens but becomes rather hard and brittle. I have several such dried bits, which I use as bookmarks in my whale-books. It is transparent, as I said before; and laying it on the printed page, I have sometimes amused myself by imagining that it had a magnifying effect. At any rate, it is pleasant to read about whales through their own spectacles, as you might say. But what I am driving at here is this. That same infinitely thin, isinglass substance, which, I admit, covers the entire body of the whale, is not so much to be regarded as the skin of the creature as the skin of the skin, so to speak; for it would be simply ridiculous to say that the proper skin of the tremendous whale is thinner and more tender than the skin of a newborn child. But no more of this.

Assuming the blubber to be the skin of the whale: when this skin, as in the case of a very large Sperm Whale, will yield the bulk of one hundred barrels of oil; and when you consider that, in quantity, or rather weight, that oil in its pressed-out state is only three-quarters, and not the entire substance, of the coat — you may get some idea from this of the enormousness of that living mass, a mere part of whose mere covering yields such a lake of liquid as that. Reckoning ten barrels to the ton, you have ten tons for the net weight of only three-quarters of the stuff of the whale's skin.

In life, the visible surface of the Sperm Whale is not the least among the many marvels he presents. Almost invariably it is obliquely crossed and re-crossed all over with countless straight marks in thick array, something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be impressed upon the isinglass substance mentioned above; rather, they seem to be seen through it, as if they were engraved upon the body itself. Nor is this all. In some instances, to the quick, observant eye, those linear marks, as in a real engraving, only provide the ground for quite other drawings. These are hieroglyphical; that is, if you call those mysterious ciphers on the walls of pyramids hieroglyphics, then that is the proper word to use here. Remembering well the hieroglyphics on one Sperm Whale in particular, I was much struck by a plate showing the old Indian characters chiseled on the famous hieroglyphic palisades on the banks of the Upper Mississippi. Like those mystic rocks, too, the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable. This allusion to the Indian rocks reminds me of another thing. Besides all the other phenomena that the exterior of the Sperm Whale presents, he quite often shows his back, and more especially his flanks, with the regular linear pattern largely effaced by numerous rough scratches, altogether irregular and random in appearance. I should say that those New England rocks on the sea-coast which Agassiz imagines to bear the marks of violent scraping contact with vast floating icebergs — I should say that those rocks must resemble the Sperm Whale not a little in this respect. It also seems to me that such scratches in the whale are probably made by hostile contact with other whales; for I have noticed them most in the large, full-grown bulls of the species.

A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces, called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is very apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better still, an Indian poncho slipped over his head and hanging down around his extremity. It is because of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is able to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of the North, if he were not supplied with his cozy overcoat? True, other fish are found to be exceedingly lively in those Hyperborean waters; but these, mind you, are your cold-blooded, lungless fish, whose very bellies are refrigerators; creatures that warm themselves in the lee of an iceberg, as a traveler in winter would bask before an inn fire; whereas, like man, the whale has lungs and warm blood. Freeze his blood, and he dies. How wonderful it is, then — unless it is explained — that this great monster, to whom bodily warmth is as indispensable as it is to man; how wonderful that he should be found at home, immersed to his lips for life in those Arctic waters! — where, when seamen fall overboard, they are sometimes found months afterward, frozen upright into the hearts of fields of ice, as a fly is found glued in amber. But it is more surprising still to know, as has been proved by experiment, that the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.

It certainly seems to me that here we see the rare virtue of a strong individual vitality, the rare virtue of thick walls, and the rare virtue of roominess within. Oh, man! Admire the whale and take him as your model! You, too, stay warm in the ice. You, too, live in this world without being of it. Stay cool at the equator; keep your blood flowing at the Pole. Like the great dome of St. Peter's, and like the great whale, keep, O man, a temperature of your own in every season.
But how easy it is to teach these fine things, and how hopeless! How few buildings have a dome like St. Peter's! How few creatures are as vast as the whale!
